text: — Oh! Bay Ganyo, Christ is risen! Were you at the palace for the breaking of the fast?

— Me, you mean? Why, if I don’t do it, who will? — replies Bay Ganyo to me, and, twirling his left mustache, gives me a sly wink, that is: “As long as there are fools in the world, your Uncle Ganyo won’t let a profit slip by.”
— Well, how did it go? Was it fun?

— Ah, who’s looking cheerful? There was profit in it, rich man! I stuffed myself like... what’s-his-name... You know, Passion Week, I fasted, I fasted, I puffed myself up with that cursed beans, and on top of that the army ration, I was as hungry as a wolf. On Saturday I didn’t put a crumb in my mouth. And then they went and set the breaking of the fast for two in the morning... While I was standing in church, it was as if three hundred leeches were sucking at my belly. You spit, you spit, and there’s no saliva left. You try to smoke — it won’t go down, it tastes bitter in your mouth... They said “Christ is risen” — it’s twelve o’clock, how are you supposed to wait until two! I told my folks to go and break their fast by themselves, and I went into “The Red Crab.” There, my brother, it was full of people like me — top hats, epaulettes, orders. And they too were waiting for two o’clock to strike. I sat down at a long table, and I see several bachelors breaking the fast. They had laid out that table of theirs with snacks, roast pig, and even Varna wine on top — enough to drip right onto your stomach. Just looking at the piglet’s skin made my head nearly fly off. Well, what, I should have asked those bachelors: “What are you eating there, eh? Pig? Bravo! Let me... what’s-his-name... a little with the skin...” — and the people would have given me some. But no. I’ve been shy since I was little... (Go on, give me your tobacco case, you smoke good tobacco, Ivanov’s is no good at all, it smells like makhorka...) Those bachelors were smacking their lips, I got sick of watching them, and I turned my eyes away. I thought I’d spit, but where was there any saliva! My guts had stuck together. I thought of ordering a beer, but I lost my appetite. Was that why I’d gone hungry for two days, as they say... I turned away so as not to look at them, but they, as if on purpose, the devil take them, kept chewing and kept praising the pig. I felt like getting up and snatching that cursed pig right out of their mouths... If only I could bend over and press my stomach a bit like that — the hunger wouldn’t be felt so much, but I can’t bend over. My frock coat is too tight, it’ll burst at the back. Ah, let the devil take it! And the collar was starched so stiff that it scraped my neck like a saw... My eyes went dark. I left the Crab and headed toward the palace. It won’t do to go in early. I have a gendarme friend there, a good friend too, if you ask me, almost a relative, but he still doesn’t quite oblige. And even if you go in early, it’s all the same, they won’t set the table for you right away. I wandered, wandered around the gates, my legs started hurting. Then at one point, drrr... one carriage, and shortly after drrr... another carriage. They went into the palace, thank God! I twirled my mustaches a bit, cleared my throat, and off I went after them. I went inside, and I see the gendarmes, the escort, already lined up. A shaved-headed boy rushed up to take off my coat, and I muttered at him: “Excuse me, sir, mind your own business,” and I didn’t let him take it off. He got embarrassed and went to undress others. How could I let him undress me, brother? The sleeves of my coat, that is, not the sleeves, but the lining inside, were torn to pieces like... what’s-his-name. Well then. I went upstairs, but before going up I cast an eye into the lower rooms — the tables were laid out, everything spotless. People gathered. We waited a little here too, and then the prince came out with the princess. This time they were, in Christian fashion, truly master and mistress of the house. They handed us each an egg...

— Well, damn... I’d have kissed a hundred hands for such a table. So be it. That ordeal passed too, for when we rushed down the stairs, brother mine... Believe it or not, I was leaping three steps at a time; I nearly smashed into the mirror, but I didn’t let anyone get ahead of me. I grabbed the caviar, and when I dug in with the spoon, if there was less than half a kilo of it — may it be a sin on my soul. That fish mayonnaise of yours, those little snacks of mine, I don’t know their names, but when those mouths opened... Never mind!... I ate, I ate, I stuffed myself... and even now I wonder how my stomach didn’t burst. And the drinking... When I left, how I left — cut me open, I don’t remember... Uff!... My head still hurts from that blasted champagne... And that’s not all, for when I started stuffing my pockets with pastries, and they were soft, the devil take them, and they got all mashed up in my pocket... Well, goodbye then.
